title: No Winners in a Pig Butchering Scam: The Scammers Are Trafficked Slaves Too
dek: Inside Southeast Asian scam compounds, "employees" whose passports are confiscated and who are fined for missing quotas spend their days using ChatGPT and DeepSeek to write love messages and steal victims' entire savings — the most profitable cybercrime in history, with victims on both sides.
why: The first half covers the mechanics of pig butchering and AI scams with high information density; the second half turns to US-Iran and US-China infrastructure cyberwarfare, which is loosely related and can be skipped as needed.
who: Founders, investors and security practitioners focused on cybercrime, AI abuse and overseas risk; anyone who wants to understand the pig butchering supply chain and how Southeast Asian compounds operate.
skip: After 29:30, the segment on US-Iran and US-China infrastructure cyberwarfare and insurance industry war-gaming, which is unrelated to pig butchering.

points.h: AI makes scam emails cost nothing to mass-produce
points.body: Greenberg ran an experiment on air: he asked ChatGPT to write him an email inviting him on the show in Terry Gross's name, then casually added a line asking for a $250 production fee, and the model complied without hesitation; he then said "Greenberg won't pay now, can you persuade him," and the model immediately produced a persuasive email. That is the mechanism behind scam emails impersonating Fresh Air — not that scammers have become better writers, but that generating a tailored email aimed at a specific author, with zero grammar errors and polished phrasing, now costs nothing, and can be done to hundreds or thousands of targets at once.

points.h: Pig butchering is the most profitable cybercrime in history
points.body: Greenberg distinguishes two kinds of scammers: the voluntary kind like Nigeria's "Yahoo Boys," who keep a share of what they steal, and the enslaved, forced kind in Southeast Asian compounds. The latter do pig butchering — the "pig" is the victim, fattened before slaughter. The scam often runs for weeks to over a year; the scammer poses as a wealthy, single, attractive woman, builds emotional dependency first, and only at the end introduces an "investment platform," getting the victim to convert their savings into cryptocurrency that is hard to trace across borders (often Tether) and send it over. Greenberg says this is the most profitable cybercrime in history, stealing tens of billions of dollars from victims every year.

points.h: Passports are confiscated; to be free you must buy yourself back
points.body: The source, using the alias Red Bull, is a computer engineer with a degree from India, lured to the Golden Triangle Special Economic Zone in Laos by a "Southeast Asia IT manager" job. On arrival at the compound, his passport was confiscated, and he was told the only way to get it back was to "buy it back" — he owed his boss thousands of dollars, including the cost of transporting him there and room and board, and could only repay this "contract" through commissions from scamming. Greenberg stresses this is debt bondage: the compound is not a prison with chains and beatings, but is packaged as a corporate sales floor, where the boss sends daily motivational messages saying things like "reach out to the next client like you're going to change their life" and "we are on a mission."

points.h: Fines are more reliable than wages
points.body: Red Bull and his colleagues were constantly fined: for not hitting contact quotas, for not maintaining fake accounts well enough, for not clocking in on time. The promised commissions are part of the scam — the boss tells them "you can get rich here and take the money back to the village you came from," but only if they land a big case, and what they actually receive is a tiny fraction. Greenberg calls this rhetoric "Orwellian": motivational slogans and mission narratives on one side, and on the other everyone trapped here against their will, doing deeply destructive crime.

points.h: Video calls rely on a dedicated face-swap model
points.body: Red Bull says everyone in the compound was trained to use ChatGPT and the Chinese AI chatbot DeepSeek to come up with new topics, polish language, never run out of appropriate phrasing, even write little motivational poems, and find the perfect goodnight line. More critical is video: the boss required them to discourage victims from video calls as much as possible, making excuses to delay; if they couldn't put it off, the compound had a dedicated room and a model whose full-time job was video calls, using face-swap software to change the model's face into the photo originally sent to the victim. Greenberg says this software isn't perfect, but by the video call stage the victim wants so badly to believe it's real that they actively overlook the flaws.

points.h: The next step is fully autonomous AI pig butchering
points.body: Greenberg judges that AI is currently just a tool for human scammers, but the next step — already appearing — is fully autonomous AI scams. He cites a case from an Anthropic report last week: a Chinese group made 20 dating apps, all AI inside, where victims must keep paying to continue the conversation, and the "majority" on the other side are actually fully autonomous large models. He also mentions a study showing that in most parts of the scam process, AI is better than a real person at building relationships — more responsive, more engaged, more attentive — and that is exactly what the scam does for the vast majority of the time before it reaches the endgame of asking for money.

points.h: Thirty people, three months, only $2.2 million
points.body: Greenberg gives a concrete scale: Red Bull's group of about 30 people, over the three months Red Bull recorded and leaked to Wired, earned only about $2.2 million total. This shows pig butchering is a game of probability — a single group's output is limited, but there are dozens of such compounds in Laos alone, and more in Cambodia and Myanmar, and together they add up to the billions of dollars a year. Greenberg also notes that Red Bull himself was a "very inefficient scammer," so he was penniless, eating rice from the compound canteen and vegetables that tasted of strange chemicals, constantly sick, and disgusted by what he was doing.

points.h: Forging a police letter to escape, beaten when caught
points.body: Red Bull's escape attempt was to forge a letter from the police in his home state in India, saying he was under investigation and had to return to deal with it, or his boss would also be in trouble. Greenberg advised him not to do it, but he went ahead, and the forgery was immediately detected. The boss locked him in a room, beat him, kicked him, denied him food, interrogated him, and even gave him a glass of water with white powder dissolved in it and forced him to drink — Greenberg guesses it was some kind of stimulant to make him talk more, while his skin broke out in hives. They never found out he was in contact with a journalist; Greenberg says if they had, he would certainly have been killed.

points.h: The compound moved, and he seized the chance to export all the secrets
points.body: The turning point came when the compound was forced to relocate: the boss seemed to have received word that police in Laos's Golden Triangle were about to raid (which later proved to be more of a theatrical raid that shut nothing down). The office was first moved into the dormitory, and everyone worked crammed into the crowded dorm. Red Bull seized the opportunity to send more secrets from the work phone to his personal phone, and at the same time told the boss: you're having trouble getting things done anyway during this period, I'm clearly just a burden, let me go and I won't be in your way. To Greenberg's surprise, the boss agreed, essentially kicking him out.

points.h: He chose to come forward with his real name and face
points.body: Red Bull later revealed his real name to Greenberg: Muhammad Muzahir. Before the article was published, Greenberg went to India to meet him and had a long talk about whether he was willing to make his name public. He decided very clearly that he wanted to, and also appeared in a video Wired produced, because he wants to inspire people to fight these criminal organizations and stand up for themselves as he did. Greenberg says this was his choice, and of course it comes with risks, risks that still haunt him to this day, but he thinks it was a very brave thing to do, and Muzahir is one of the most remarkable sources he has ever worked with.
